power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Neurodevelopmental conditions (NDCs) arise from complex genetic-environmental interactions, yet their molecular underpinnings remain incompletely defined.
We applied an integrative multi-omics approach within a deeply phenotyped twin cohort to identify systemic molecular signatures and pathways associated with NDCs.

Our study included 237 twins aged 8-28 years from the Roots of Autism and ADHD Twin Study in Sweden (RATSS), with one or more omics layers available per individual, including serum and cerebrospinal fluid proteomics, urine and fecal metabolomics, blood metallomics, and whole-genome sequencing in a subset of 14 monozygotic (MZ) twin pairs.
Using the DIABLO framework, we identified cross-omics features that distinguish individuals with and without NDCs.
The identified features converged on enriched metabolic and immune-related pathways, including purine metabolism, lysine degradation, PI3K-Akt, and MAPK signaling.
Several key molecules also showed differential abundance at the single-molecule level in generalized estimating equation (GEE) models.

ADA protein, pyrimidine-related metabolites (thymidine, glutamine, and 2'-deoxyuridine), and copper showed suggestive associations within NDC-discordant MZ twin pairs, pointing to potential non-shared condition-related effects, while flavin mononucleotide and manganese associations with NDCs were influenced by shared genetic or familial environmental factors.
Our findings indicate that NDC-related molecular alterations manifest across multiple biological layers and tissues, and are detectable through integrative systems-level analysis.

Our scalable framework provides critical insights into altered metabolic and immune processes in NDCs and highlights candidate features that may inform future biomarker development and mechanistic research in precision psychiatry.

Neurodevelopmental conditions (NDCs), such as autism, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), motor and language disorders, are defined by cognitive and behavioral difficulties causing functional challenges in social, academic, and occupational arenas [1].
text.formatted: Neurodevelopmental conditions (NDCs), such as autism, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), motor and language disorders, are defined by cognitive and behavioral difficulties causing functional challenges in social, academic, and occupational arenas <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: In high-income countries, approximately 15% of children aged 3 to 17 years are diagnosed with NDCs [2], which exhibit pronounced heterogeneity while sharing clinical features across diagnoses [3] [4] [5].
text.formatted: In high-income countries, approximately 15% of children aged 3 to 17 years are diagnosed with NDCs <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>, which exhibit pronounced heterogeneity while sharing clinical features across diagnoses <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: Sex and gender are also important contributors to the biological and behavioral variability [6].
text.formatted: Sex and gender are also important contributors to the biological and behavioral variability <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: NDC diagnoses frequently co-occur, and individuals with NDCs are also at increased risk for somatic and psychiatric disorders [1, 7].
text.formatted: NDC diagnoses frequently co-occur, and individuals with NDCs are also at increased risk for somatic and psychiatric disorders <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7]</ref>.

text.text: Although the origins, physiological mechanisms, and consequences of NDCs remain incompletely understood, both genetic and environmental factors contribute substantially to NDC liability, with heritability estimates from 0.66 across conditions to approximately 0.83 for autism specifically in children and adolescents [8, 9].
text.formatted: Although the origins, physiological mechanisms, and consequences of NDCs remain incompletely understood, both genetic and environmental factors contribute substantially to NDC liability, with heritability estimates from 0.66 across conditions to approximately 0.83 for autism specifically in children and adolescents <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9]</ref>.

text.text: Metabolic, immune, and inflammatory factors also contribute to NDC likelihood and may interact with genetic susceptibility, further complicating their etiology [10] [11] [12] [13].
text.formatted: Metabolic, immune, and inflammatory factors also contribute to NDC likelihood and may interact with genetic susceptibility, further complicating their etiology <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>.

text.text: Single-omics studies have contributed to elucidating the biological underpinnings of NDCs.

Genomic research has identified hundreds of NDC-associated genes enriched for rare and de novo variants [14] [15] [16], many of which disrupt transcriptional regulation, synaptic function, and brain development [17] [18] [19].
text.formatted: Genomic research has identified hundreds of NDC-associated genes enriched for rare and de novo variants <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref>, many of which disrupt transcriptional regulation, synaptic function, and brain development <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref>.

text.text: Proteomic analyses of peripheral blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) have revealed altered expression profiles linked to mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammation, and metabolic processes in NDCs, with some proteins correlating with clinical symptoms [20, 21].
text.formatted: Proteomic analyses of peripheral blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) have revealed altered expression profiles linked to mitochondrial dysfunction, neuroinflammation, and metabolic processes in NDCs, with some proteins correlating with clinical symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21]</ref>.

text.text: Because metabolic alterations are sensitive to gene-environment interactions, they offer particular promise for understanding NDC physiology [22, 23].
text.formatted: Because metabolic alterations are sensitive to gene-environment interactions, they offer particular promise for understanding NDC physiology <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23]</ref>.

text.text: Metabolomic analyses of non-invasive biospecimens, such as fecal and urine samples, have demonstrated altered microbial-host co-metabolism and amino acid signatures in children with NDCs [24, 25].
text.formatted: Metabolomic analyses of non-invasive biospecimens, such as fecal and urine samples, have demonstrated altered microbial-host co-metabolism and amino acid signatures in children with NDCs <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25]</ref>.

text.text: Despite the breadth of reported molecular associations, no highly reliable NDC biomarker has been established [26].
text.formatted: Despite the breadth of reported molecular associations, no highly reliable NDC biomarker has been established <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref>.

text.text: Growing omics datasets increasingly enable integration of multiple molecular layers to investigate the complex interplay between biological systems.
However, applications in NDC research have only recently emerged [27].
text.formatted: However, applications in NDC research have only recently emerged <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27]</ref>.

text.text: Early efforts typically combined two or three omics layers, most commonly archived genome-wide data with proteomic or transcriptomic data, to assess how genetic variants shape NDC physiology through altered gene or protein expression [28].
text.formatted: Early efforts typically combined two or three omics layers, most commonly archived genome-wide data with proteomic or transcriptomic data, to assess how genetic variants shape NDC physiology through altered gene or protein expression <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28]</ref>.

text.text: Metabolomics has frequently complemented these layers by linking molecular changes to functional pathways.

In autism, integrated urine metabolomic and proteomic analyses implicated altered neuroimmune pathways [29], while crosstissue meta-analyses identified shared molecular signatures across the central nervous system, circulatory system, and non-invasive biofluids [30].
text.formatted: In autism, integrated urine metabolomic and proteomic analyses implicated altered neuroimmune pathways <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref>, while crosstissue meta-analyses identified shared molecular signatures across the central nervous system, circulatory system, and non-invasive biofluids <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref>.

text.text: Despite limited sample sizes, integration of placental transcriptomics and metabolomics has shown diagnostic promise, with a machine-learning model classifying NDCs at >95% accuracy using only a few components [31].
text.formatted: Despite limited sample sizes, integration of placental transcriptomics and metabolomics has shown diagnostic promise, with a machine-learning model classifying NDCs at >95% accuracy using only a few components <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref>.

text.text: Recently, urine metabolomics combined with genomics and epigenomics revealed differential association patterns in ADHD, including strong correlations between specific CpG loci and ADHD polygenic scores [32].
text.formatted: Recently, urine metabolomics combined with genomics and epigenomics revealed differential association patterns in ADHD, including strong correlations between specific CpG loci and ADHD polygenic scores <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32]</ref>.

text.text: Beyond traditional omics layers, incorporating nutritional status and toxic metal exposure may more directly connect molecular findings to modifiable dietary and environmental factors in the etiology of NDC [33].
text.formatted: Beyond traditional omics layers, incorporating nutritional status and toxic metal exposure may more directly connect molecular findings to modifiable dietary and environmental factors in the etiology of NDC <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33]</ref>.

text.text: Both essential metals (e.g., copper, manganese, and zinc) and toxic metals (e.g., lead, mercury, and arsenic) can influence brain development and function, as altered homeostasis or disrupted metabolic pathways may affect neuronal function and contribute to neurodevelopmental phenotypes [34] [35] [36] [37].
text.formatted: Both essential metals (e.g., copper, manganese, and zinc) and toxic metals (e.g., lead, mercury, and arsenic) can influence brain development and function, as altered homeostasis or disrupted metabolic pathways may affect neuronal function and contribute to neurodevelopmental phenotypes <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[34]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">[36]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[37]</ref>.

text.text: However, comprehensive frameworks that integrate multi-tissue, multi-omics data collected within the same cohort, including less-explored domains such as metallomics, remain rare.
Twin study designs provide a uniquely powerful framework for isolating condition-associated biological variation from shared genetic and environmental confounding.

By controlling for age and most of the early-life environment and, in monozygotic (MZ) pairs, for essentially the entire inherited genome, within-pair comparisons substantially reduce background sources of heterogeneity.
Consequently, differences observed in condition-discordant twin pairs can be more confidently attributed to conditionrelated processes rather than shared genetic or environmental influences [38, 39].
text.formatted: Consequently, differences observed in condition-discordant twin pairs can be more confidently attributed to conditionrelated processes rather than shared genetic or environmental influences <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">[38,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">39]</ref>.

text.text: In this exploratory study, we applied an integrative multi-omics approach with a twin design to identify molecular signatures and convergent biological pathways associated with NDCs across multiple layers of biological organization.

We leveraged data from the Roots of Autism and ADHD Twin Study in Sweden (RATSS) cohort [40, 41], which includes twin pairs concordant and discordant for NDCs, as well as typically developing twin pairs.
text.formatted: We leveraged data from the Roots of Autism and ADHD Twin Study in Sweden (RATSS) cohort <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[40,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41]</ref>, which includes twin pairs concordant and discordant for NDCs, as well as typically developing twin pairs.

text.text: By integrating complementary single-omics datasets generated from the RATSS cohort, including serum and CSF proteomics [21], fecal and urine metabolomics [24], blood metallomics, and whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data from a subset of 14 MZ twin pairs, we systematically examined cross-omics relationships and biological convergence across molecular layers.
text.formatted: By integrating complementary single-omics datasets generated from the RATSS cohort, including serum and CSF proteomics <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref>, fecal and urine metabolomics <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref>, blood metallomics, and whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data from a subset of 14 MZ twin pairs, we systematically examined cross-omics relationships and biological convergence across molecular layers.

text.text: The most important molecules were examined using across-and within-twin-pair analyses to highlight genetic and environmental contributions.
The sample was drawn from RATSS [40, 41], a deeply phenotyped cohort of twin pairs with various NDC diagnoses and neurotypically developing twins (Supplementary Fig. S1, Table S1).
text.formatted: The sample was drawn from RATSS <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[40,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41]</ref>, a deeply phenotyped cohort of twin pairs with various NDC diagnoses and neurotypically developing twins (Supplementary Fig. <ref type="figure">S1</ref>, Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref>).

text.text: Detailed recruitment, clinical assessment, and behavioral measures are described in Supplementary Methods S1 and in previous publications [40, 41].
text.formatted: Detailed recruitment, clinical assessment, and behavioral measures are described in Supplementary Methods S1 and in previous publications <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[40,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">41]</ref>.

text.text: Briefly, twins were recruited from a population-based twin cohort and other sources, targeting autism and ADHD discordant pairs.

All twins underwent a comprehensive behavioral assessment at a clinical research center (Supplementary Methods S2), including ageappropriate parent-rated Child/Adult Behavior Checklist (CBCL/ABCL), self-rated Youth/Adult Behavior
Responsiveness Scale 2nd Edition (SRS-2), Wechsler Intelligence Scales (WISC-IV/WAIS-IV) or the Leiter scales.
NDCs and psychiatric disorders were assessed by expert-clinician consensus according to DSM-5 and ICD-10 criteria [1].
text.formatted: NDCs and psychiatric disorders were assessed by expert-clinician consensus according to DSM-5 and ICD-10 criteria <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: Zygosity was determined by genotyping or a 48-single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) panel [42, 43].
text.formatted: Zygosity was determined by genotyping or a 48-single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) panel <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">[42,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">43]</ref>.

text.text: A subset of 14 MZ twin pairs provided WGS data as part of the EU-AIMS initiative [44].
text.formatted: A subset of 14 MZ twin pairs provided WGS data as part of the EU-AIMS initiative <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">[44]</ref>.

text.text: NDC discordance was defined by one twin meeting DSM-5/ICD-10 criteria for any NDC (e.g., autism, ADHD, Intellectual Disability [ID], Tic Disorder, and Specific Learning Disorder) while the co-twin did not.
Individuals with one or more NDC diagnoses were assigned to the anyNDC group, and those without any to the noNDC group.
The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the Swedish Ethical Review Authority (2016/145-231).
Informed consent was obtained from all participants and/or their caregivers.
Serum and CSF proteomic data were available for 126 and 86 individuals, respectively.
Proteins were measured using multiplex immunoassay panels (Olink Bioscience, Sweden; RRID:SCR_003899), including Inflammation I, CVD (cardiovascular), and Oncology I, covering 203 proteins.
More details are provided in Supplementary Methods S3.1 and Smedler et al. [21].
text.formatted: More details are provided in Supplementary Methods S3.1 and Smedler et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref>.

text.text: Urine and fecal metabolomic data were available for 112 and 189 individuals, respectively.
Urine was profiled by untargeted 1 H nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, and fecal samples by untargeted liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (Metabolon).
More details are provided in Supplementary Methods S3.2, S3.3 and Swann et al. [24].
text.formatted: More details are provided in Supplementary Methods S3.2, S3.3 and Swann et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref>.

text.text: Metallomic profiling was performed on blood samples from 220 individuals, quantifying essential [calcium (Ca), copper (Cu), iron (Fe), magnesium (Mg), manganese (Mn), molybdenum (Mo), selenium (Se), and zinc (Zn)] and toxic metals [arsenic (As), cadmium (Cd), cobalt (Co), mercury (Hg), and lead (Pb)] by inductively coupled plasma-mass spectrometry (ICP-MS).
More details are provided in Supplementary Methods S3.4.

We applied an integrative multi-omics strategy using the DIABLO (Data Integration Analysis for Biomarker Discovery using Latent Variable Approaches for Omics Studies) framework implemented in the R package mixOmics (version 6.22.0) [45].
text.formatted: We applied an integrative multi-omics strategy using the DIABLO (Data Integration Analysis for Biomarker Discovery using Latent Variable Approaches for Omics Studies) framework implemented in the R package mixOmics (version 6.22.0) <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">[45]</ref>.

text.text: DIABLO applied multiblock sparse Partial Least Squares Discriminant Analysis (sPLS-DA) to identify molecules correlated across omics layers while jointly contributing to discriminating anyNDC from noNDC.
Through LASSO penalization, a sparse subset of molecules was selected, producing latent components (variates) for each omics block.
Each individual received a variate score for each component per block, reflecting their position along the axis of maximal cross-omics covariation associated with NDC status.
The average variate 1 and variate 2 scores across omics blocks indicate cross-omics NDC-associated separation at the individual level.
We first applied single-omics sPLS-DA models to optimize variable selection parameters for each dataset.

To maximize sample coverage across diverse omics combinations, we designed three complementary multi-omics models: MultiOmic-SCFB (serum-proteomics, CSF-proteomics, fecal-metabolomics, and bloodmetallomics datasets) with 72 samples (37 anyNDC, 35 noNDC); MultiOmic-SFB (serum-proteomics, fecal-metabolomics, and blood-metallomics datasets) with 109 samples (56 anyNDC, 53 noNDC); MultiOmic-UFB (urine-metabolomics, fecal-metabolomics, and blood-metallomics datasets) with 89 samples (29 anyNDC, 60 noNDC) (Fig. 1, Supplementary Fig. S2).
text.formatted: To maximize sample coverage across diverse omics combinations, we designed three complementary multi-omics models: MultiOmic-SCFB (serum-proteomics, CSF-proteomics, fecal-metabolomics, and bloodmetallomics datasets) with 72 samples (37 anyNDC, 35 noNDC); MultiOmic-SFB (serum-proteomics, fecal-metabolomics, and blood-metallomics datasets) with 109 samples (56 anyNDC, 53 noNDC); MultiOmic-UFB (urine-metabolomics, fecal-metabolomics, and blood-metallomics datasets) with 89 samples (29 anyNDC, 60 noNDC) (Fig. <ref type="figure">1</ref>, Supplementary Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">S2</ref>).

text.text: Detailed data processing and model construction are described in Supplementary Methods S4 and Fig. S3.
text.formatted: Detailed data processing and model construction are described in Supplementary Methods S4 and Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">S3</ref>.

text.text: Associations between average variate scores and potential confounders and clinical measures were assessed using Generalized Estimating Equation (GEE) models with the R package drgee (version 1.1.10) [46] to account for the family linkage.
text.formatted: Associations between average variate scores and potential confounders and clinical measures were assessed using Generalized Estimating Equation (GEE) models with the R package drgee (version 1.1.10) <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">[46]</ref> to account for the family linkage.

text.text: We analyzed the enrichment of proteins and metabolites selected from the multi-omics models across Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathways [47] using MetaboAnalyst 6.0 web tool (accessed 2025-08-12) [48], via the Joint Pathway Analysis module.
text.formatted: We analyzed the enrichment of proteins and metabolites selected from the multi-omics models across Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathways <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">[47]</ref> using MetaboAnalyst 6.0 web tool (accessed 2025-08-12) <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">[48]</ref>, via the Joint Pathway Analysis module.

text.text: Using the default background, we evaluated both metabolic-pathway and all-pathway libraries.
Enrichment significance was determined by a hypergeometric test, with degree centrality as a topology measure to weight individual molecular importance.

We applied different integration methods for the background: for metabolic pathway analysis, the "Overall Combine p values" method, which weights the proportion of each omics; for all pathway analysis, the tighter "Combine Query" method, which pools the genes/proteins and metabolites into a single query.
The false discovery rate (FDR) method was used to correct for multiple comparisons [49].
text.formatted: The false discovery rate (FDR) method was used to correct for multiple comparisons <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">[49]</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, we applied Gene-Metabolite Interaction Network analysis in the Network Analysis module (default parameters) to examine interactions between selected proteins and metabolites.

We selected seven metals that showed correlation coefficients > 0.6 with features from other omics layers in multi-omics models, including the essential metals Ca, Mg, Fe, Zn, and Mn, as well as the toxic metals Co and Cd.
text.formatted: We selected seven metals that showed correlation coefficients > 0.6 with features from other omics layers in multi-omics models, including the essential metals Ca, Mg, Fe, Zn, and Mn, as well as the toxic metals Co and Cd.

text.text: In the Comparative Toxicogenomics Database (CTD, accessed 2025-01-09) [50], we searched the condition keyword "neurodevelopmental disorder" and retrieved curated gene sets for each metal with a documented association with NDCs.
text.formatted: In the Comparative Toxicogenomics Database (CTD, accessed 2025-01-09) <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">[50]</ref>, we searched the condition keyword "neurodevelopmental disorder" and retrieved curated gene sets for each metal with a documented association with NDCs.

text.text: Ca was excluded because its association with NDCs in CTD lacked curated evidence.
We then conducted KEGG pathway enrichment analysis on the combined gene lists using the R package clusterProfiler (version 4.6.2) [51], with p-values adjusted by the FDR method.
text.formatted: We then conducted KEGG pathway enrichment analysis on the combined gene lists using the R package clusterProfiler (version 4.6.2) <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">[51]</ref>, with p-values adjusted by the FDR method.

text.text: To assess associations between molecular levels and NDC diagnosis, we focused on molecules mapped to significantly enriched metabolic pathways and all 13 metals.
The lysine degradation pathway was additionally included as it reached nominal significance in the protein-metabolite pathway analysis and FDR-significance in the metal-related pathway analysis.

We first assessed across-individual effects using standard GEE models adjusted for age, sex, BMI, medication (yes/no), and other psychiatric diagnosis (yes/no), with standard errors clustered by twin pair.

To control for unmeasured family-constant confounders (e.g., parental psychiatric history, growth environment, and shared genetic factors of twin pairs), we then applied conditional GEE (CGEE) models to estimate within-pair molecular effects.
CGEE models were adjusted for cluster-varying covariates (BMI, medication, and other psychiatric diagnoses).
Analyses were performed across all twin pairs, MZ twin pairs, and NDC-discordant MZ pairs to isolate the effects of non-shared exposures.
We analyzed WGS data from 14 MZ twin pairs (3 NDC-discordant, 6 NDC-concordant, and 5 noNDCconcordant pairs).
Zygosity was confirmed by kinship coefficient analysis (Kinship >0.345).
text.formatted: Zygosity was confirmed by kinship coefficient analysis (Kinship >0.345).

In this study, we applied an integrative multi-omics strategy within a twin cohort, combining data-driven multiblock sPLS-DA models with knowledge-based pathway enrichment to investigate molecular signatures and biological pathways associated with NDC.
Convergent signals implicated several metabolic and signaling pathways across omics layers.

Twin-model-based analyses provided additional context for the molecules prioritized by the integrative framework, indicating that their associations with NDC arose from a combination of shared genetic/familial influences and non-shared individualspecific factors across different molecular features.

ADA protein and blood copper showed independent associations with NDC status, while thymidine, glutamine, and 2'-deoxyuridine, involved in pyrimidine metabolism, were consistently decreased in the NDC-discordant MZ subset.
Flavin mononucleotide and blood manganese were also associated with NDC, though their associations were modulated by shared genetic or familial environmental influences.

A key value of the integrative approach is that some molecules' relevance to NDC becomes apparent only through their correlation with other omics layers rather than from single-omics testing alone [54].

WGS, although available only in 14 MZ twin pairs, complements these insights by capturing rare genetic variation at both somatic and germline levels, offering a genetic-layer perspective on processes also highlighted at the physiological level.
Molecules highlighted by both the integrative models and individual-level differential analysis are considered doubly supported and given particular weight in our discussion.
Several pathways were consistently and significantly implicated across different omics layers, highlighting their potential involvement in NDC physiology.
Among metabolic pathways, lysine degradation emerged as the most consistently enriched process.

Numerous studies have associated lysine degradation with mitochondrial energy metabolism and redox homeostasis; however, direct evidence linking it to NDC remains limited and mainly focused on autism.

text.text: The accumulation of 2-aminoadipate is of particular interest because it can act as a neurotoxin by inhibiting the synthesis of kynurenic acid, a neuroprotective metabolite.
Such accumulation may occur when aminotransferases that normally metabolize 2-aminoadipate are impaired, a process dependent on the cofactor pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (PLP, vitamin B6).
Reduced or highly variable PLP levels have been reported in some autistic children compared with the neurotypical group [60].

text.text: Together, these findings highlight a potential microbial-host metabolic axis linking lysine degradation, vitamin B6-dependent enzymatic activity, and neurobehavioral regulation in NDCs.
The purine metabolism pathway also emerged as a key metabolic focus in our study, enriched across multiple layers.
This pathway is critically involved in neurodevelopment, particularly through its regulation of neuroimmune interactions and oxidative stress responses [63].

text.text: Our finding of elevated serum ADA in NDC group parallels this molecular trend and remained robust even after controlling for family-constant confounding.
Notably, CSF ADA levels did not differ between groups, reflecting region-specific regulation of ADA in peripheral metabolic disturbances.

Together, we extend prior genetic-and transcriptomiclevel observations to the protein level and broaden ADA's relevance across NDC diagnoses, highlighting ADA as a potential peripheral biomarker of purine metabolic imbalance in NDC.
The purine metabolism pathway also appears to interact with broader neuroimmune signaling networks implicated in NDCs.
In our metabolite-protein interaction network, adenosine, the central node of purine metabolism, exhibited close topological proximity to several members of the chemokine family.
Consistent with this, the chemokine signaling pathway was also significantly enriched in our proteinmetabolite joint pathway analysis and in the gene set harboring rare unique variants found in NDCs.
Chemokines are well-established mediators of neuroimmune signaling, and their dysregulation during early development has been linked to altered neurodevelopmental trajectories in autism [68].

text.text: These findings suggest a potential mechanistic convergence between purinergic signaling and immune modulation in the context of NDCs.
Our findings also highlighted several other key cell-signaling pathways, most notably the PI3K-Akt and MAPK signaling.
These pathways showed consistent associations across multiple data layers, involving proteins, metals, and genes carrying NDC-specific rare unique variants.
Both pathways are welldocumented regulators of neurodevelopmental processes, including neuronal survival, synaptic plasticity, and neuroimmune signaling [69, 70].

Among metabolites mapped to significantly enriched metabolic pathways, only thymidine, glutamine, and 2'-deoxyuridine, all involved in pyrimidine metabolism, were significantly lower in twins with NDCs than their unaffected co-twins in the within-pair CGEE model.
This pattern suggests that alterations in specific components of pyrimidine metabolism may contribute to NDC liability independently of genetic or shared environmental influences.
Glutamine, which is also modulated downstream of purine metabolism, has received considerable attention in NDC research due to its role in neurotransmitter balance.
It cooperates with glutamate and GABA, which are crucial for maintaining excitatory-inhibitory homeostasis in the developing brain [75].

text.text: Among other differential findings, FMN levels were strongly negatively associated with NDC in the across-individual models, but not in the within-pair analysis, suggesting that shared genetic factors may mediate the relationship.

While direct links between FMN and NDC are currently lacking, FMN serves as a critical cofactor for redox-active enzymes and ribonucleotide reductase [76] and may indirectly impact biological processes relevant to NDC physiology.
text.formatted: While direct links between FMN and NDC are currently lacking, FMN serves as a critical cofactor for redox-active enzymes and ribonucleotide reductase <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">[76]</ref> and may indirectly impact biological processes relevant to NDC physiology.

text.text: In the within-pair model, the only metal that remained significantly associated with NDC was copper.
Previous studies have reported elevated serum copper in autistic individuals, possibly contributing to oxidative stress [77].
text.formatted: Previous studies have reported elevated serum copper in autistic individuals, possibly contributing to oxidative stress <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">[77]</ref>.

text.text: However, our within-pair CGEE model employed a reduced sample size, especially for the discordant MZ twin subset, which diminished statistical power and increased the risk of false negatives.
Incorporating metallomics into the multi-omics framework offers valuable insights into environmental contributions to NDC mechanisms.
In the differential metal profiles, we found that blood manganese levels were elevated across NDC individuals within the MZ subsample but were influenced by shared genetic or environmental factors.
This may help explain part of the inconsistency in epidemiological studies of manganese exposure and NDC liability [78].
text.formatted: This may help explain part of the inconsistency in epidemiological studies of manganese exposure and NDC liability <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">[78]</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, polymorphisms in Mn-transporter genes have been shown to modulate manganese homeostasis and be associated with neurodevelopmental outcomes [79].
text.formatted: Indeed, polymorphisms in Mn-transporter genes have been shown to modulate manganese homeostasis and be associated with neurodevelopmental outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">[79]</ref>.

text.text: When genetic influence is not considered, blood manganese concentrations are generally not correlated with ingested manganese through drinking water and food [80].
text.formatted: When genetic influence is not considered, blood manganese concentrations are generally not correlated with ingested manganese through drinking water and food <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">[80]</ref>.

text.text: Associations between blood manganese and NDC also converge with pathways highlighted earlier.

In newborn rats, early-life oral manganese intake has been linked to attention deficits via dysregulation of gene expression in the prefrontal cortex, potentially involving mTOR signaling and neuroinflammatory mechanisms [81].
text.formatted: In newborn rats, early-life oral manganese intake has been linked to attention deficits via dysregulation of gene expression in the prefrontal cortex, potentially involving mTOR signaling and neuroinflammatory mechanisms <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">[81]</ref>.

text.text: In addition, manganese overexposure may disrupt neurodevelopment through oxidative stress and neuroinflammation, which are also implicated in ADA function and purine metabolism [78].
text.formatted: In addition, manganese overexposure may disrupt neurodevelopment through oxidative stress and neuroinflammation, which are also implicated in ADA function and purine metabolism <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">[78]</ref>.

text.text: Our findings underscore the complex and multilayered involvement of metal biology in pathways relevant to NDCs.
Our study has several limitations.
First, our integrative multi-omics approach provides insights into NDCassociated candidate pathways.
Still, it does not directly identify validated biomarkers or provide a predictive clinical model.

Second, although substantial for a multi-omics twin design, our sample size limits our power to detect subtle cross-omics effects and to generalize to diverse populations, particularly within NDC diagnostic subgroups.
Third, the scope and complexity of multi-omics outputs preclude exhaustive reporting, introducing potential selective emphasis in our discussion [82].
text.formatted: Third, the scope and complexity of multi-omics outputs preclude exhaustive reporting, introducing potential selective emphasis in our discussion <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">[82]</ref>.

text.text: Fourth, WGS was limited to 14 MZ twin pairs, constraining variant-discovery power and generalizability, while proteomics was restricted to targeted Olink panels, potentially biasing findings toward represented pathways.
Discordance status may also change over time, so some "discordant" pairs could reflect differences in NDC onset timing rather than stable biological discordance.

Although no significant associations emerged between DIABLO variate scores and covariates after FDR correction, nominal associations were observed between age and variate 1, and between medication and variate 2; we cannot entirely rule out these as potential sources of residual confounding in the multi-omics signature.
Future studies would benefit from untargeted proteome-wide screens and additional omics layers (e.g., transcriptomics, epigenomics) alongside richer phenotypic data.
In conclusion, this study presents a multi-omics framework embedded within a twin-cohort design to uncover potential coordinated molecular alterations underlying NDC.

The convergence of signals across metabolomic, proteomic, blood metallomic, and genetic layers points to shared biological processes involving systemic metabolic dysregulation and immune-related signaling cascades.

Notably, we observed several molecules that have not been well characterized in the NDC context (e.g., the ADA protein and FMN), and emphasized that differential molecular levels may reflect underlying genetic or shared environmental influences rather than direct effects of NDCs.

While limitations such as modest sample size constrain the generalizability of our conclusions, this study establishes a scalable framework for systems-level investigation and offers insights that may guide future biomarker discovery, liability stratification, and pathway-targeted interventions in NDC. innovation programme and EFPIA and AUTISM SPEAKS, Autistica, SFARI.
